The topic of brain chemistry is extremely complex and I won't try to pass myself by someone that really understand this issues. But I have read a book about dopamine recently that really resonated with me: <a href="https://a.co/d/4wQfKW6" alt="Dopamine Nation: Finding Balance in the Age of Indulgence" target="_blank">Dopamine Nation: Finding Balance in the Age of Indulgence</a>

This book explores the role of dopamine, a neurotransmitter associated with pleasure and reward, in our modern lives. Dr. Anna Lembke, a psychiatrist and addiction specialist, discusses how our constant exposure to stimuli like social media, food, and drugs can lead to excessive dopamine release and contribute to various forms of addiction. I always had this naive definition of addiction in my mind:

>**_If you do something and you think to yourself: 'I should probably stop doing that', you are addicted._**

Under that definition, probability says... we are all addicted to something, either a substance or a behaviour. This is how I approached the concept while going throught the book.

In the book, Lembke delves into the neuroscience of addiction and provides insights into how individuals can regain control over their dopamine-driven behaviors and find a healthier balance in an age of constant stimulation. She offers strategies for managing these impulses and making more mindful choices in our daily lives.

# Dopamine fasting

Dopamine is more associate with the willing of doing stuff, the anticipated reward. Is the force that pushes you to do something. There are several studies made with rats (for example, <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC18425/" alt="Feeding behavior in dopamine-deficient mice" target="_blank">this one</a>, or <a href="https://www.jneurosci.org/content/23/34/10827" alt="Reward without Dopamine" target="_blank">this other one</a>), where they substracted dopamine for the subjects. The rats died fairly quick (that was more or less expected), but not only that, the rats lacked the will to eat. They might eat if the food is placed directly in their mouths, but they lack the motivation to seek out food even if it's nearby. Without dopamine, there is no will for doing nothing, even to eat.

So, yes, dopamine is important, crucial to our survival. These ancient circuits in our brains say _'yes, more of that'_ and have contributed to the survival of the species. But now we live in an age of abundance. There is no need anymore to highly reward our senses each time we eat a fruit because fruit is just available. Now when we get this dopamine hit when eating a fruit, we just want more of that and quickly switch to plain and simple sugar. Our brains respond, _'oh, that's even better, more of that!'_ and the rest is pretty much history. Next thing you know, you are struggling not to eat the next doughnut.

Althought the term 'Dopamine Fasting' is often attribute to addictive technologies such as social media and Internet technologies, the definition on the book is broarder. The author uses the word DOPAMINE as an accronim to explain the theory behind dopamine fasting.

# Data

D stands for Data. Just gather some data on your consumptions habits. Either it is social media, tv, drugs... think about **what** it is, **how much** and **how often.**

# Objectives

O stands for Objectives. What are your reasons for using? The consumption is a behaviour directed to a goal, an objective. Ask why, be curious of your own habits.

# Problems

P stands for Problems. What are the downsides? Ok, you do A because of B but then you get this nasty side effect... C. You may obtain your goal for a while, for example, alcohol reduces anxiety at first. Just before to make it even worse. Any addiction has a reason to exist but then while trying to fix that problem it generates some new one, most of the times, even bigger than the original one.

# Abstinence

A stands for Abstinence. Next step is cut the consumption of the substance or the behaviour in order to restablish the normal balance in your brain between pleasure and pain. The author makes very clear that this step is not suggested to individuals who might be at risk to suffer life-threatening withdrawal if they were to quit all of a sudden, as in cases of severe alcohol, benzodiazepine (Xanax, Valium, or Klonopin), or opioid dependence and withdrawal. So, if this is your case, don't try and go to a 'dopamine fasting' and quit just like that. For those cases, medically monitored tapering is necessary.

# Mindfulness

M stands for Mindfulness. We use those substances of behaviour to scape from reality. Mindfulness is simply the ability to observe what our brain is doing while it’s doing it, without judgment. This is trickier than it sounds. Being here and now will remove the need to scape.

# Insight

I stands for Insight. Cutting on those behaviours or habits of consumption provide the insight you lack to understand your behaviour. After the abstinence it is normal to have a moment of clarity that allows you to see things with a better perspective.

# Next steps

N stands for Next steps. After the abstinence, are you able to engage in the behaviour in a moderate way or do you need to keep going with the abstinence. This is the moment to decide how do you want to go from now on.

# Experiment

E stands for Experiment. Now you have a new base line for your dopamine. You have gathered some insight from the data and the experience. You may have a plan for your next steps. It is time to experiment and maybe tackled the next potential improvement in your life.

# My personal experience

The concept of _Dopamine fasting_ stayed with me after reading the book. I was just about to start my family vacation, and that is always a challenge. Don't get me wrong; I love that time away with my family, but my children are at those ages where they can be a pain sometimes. They get bored and bother each other; they fight sometimes. Without the common distractions of their own house, it can be really delicate, especially in the first few days.

I linked this 'lack of distractions' with the book I just read. As explained in the book, the overconsumption of social media that we are witnessing these days is distracting us from the real world and also giving us a mini dopamine hit every time we scroll down. We can really get addicted to distracting ourselves, moving further and further away from reality. Remembering past years' vacations, I noticed that after a couple of days, the kids' behavior was excellent again. Was that a mini dopamine adjustment?

All right, kids are kids, and they do what they do, but what about myself? I don't use social media much, but I read. I read a lot. I can safely say that sometimes I use reading as a distraction. If I am at the supermarket queue, I don't scroll through Facebook, but I do open my e-books app and read a few pages. That may be my dopamine hit, my way to voluntarily 'erase myself' from the here and now, my way to ignore what is happening around me when what is happening is not - let's say - ideal.

The same thing happens to me when listening to podcasts. I normally listen to podcasts when doing household chores like cleaning, cooking, etc. But sometimes when I finish those tasks, I keep going with my headphones on, looking for new stuff to do just to 'keep being distracted.'

I made a conscious decision this vacation to not avoid reality by reading and listening to podcasts, trying to modify my dopamine level to a more reasonable baseline. So, I only read my book before going to sleep, and I didn't listen to podcasts at all during the whole time. I also didn't drink any alcohol during the whole period.

The improvement was really surprising. The quality of the time spent with my family increased considerably, this was my 'insight' moment. I cannot stress enough how much better the experience was compared to previous years. I think that cutting off drinking really made a difference. I don't know if it's the age or what, but nowadays I get a bit grumpy when I drink, so after my positive vacation experience, I cut back more and more, and today I am actually only drinking on big occasions like birthdays, weddings, and such; and even then, just one or two glasses of something soft.

I am definitely going to repeat this process for the next vacations, but not only that, I am trying slowly to incorporate this technique into my day-to-day life. Trying to be in the moment, in the here and now, is the cure for most worries and a simple (though not easy) way to really improve your life.
